messages.subject: Re: Combining aerial photography and MRDS
messages.body_plain:
Hi folks,

Thanks for the replies (copied below). Regarding David and Len=E2=80=99s =
suggestion of setting up =E2=80=9Ctrials=E2=80=9D for the visual observer=
s using the photos and then doing a Trial-observer MRDS analysis, one pro=
blem I can foresee is that we had high densities in relatively open water=
, near sea ice, and very low densities in sea ice. Detection in open wate=
r is much easier than detection in sea ice. So, we definitely need to set=
 up some trials in sea ice to check if the low densities are true low den=
sities or a lack of detection due to sea ice.

I=E2=80=99m going to spend some time reading up on Trial-observer MRDS an=
d may post a follow-up question at a later time.

Thanks for all of your help thus far,
Natalie.=20

Reply 1:

September 26, 2011

Any use of the photos to "correct" the visual observations would have to =
assume that: 1. all narwhal visible to observers are visible on the photo=
s; and 2. Photoanalysts do not miss narwhal that are visible on the photo=
s.=20

I don't think either of these assumptions is necessarily true for narwhal=
. For 1), observers might see animals ahead of the plane that were not vi=
sible on the photos, or the observers may detect the animal through movem=
ent but this would not be detectable on still photos. For 2), we all know=
 observers miss animals, so why would we expect observers looking at phot=
os not to? This could however be estimated by taking a couple of blind pa=
sses through the photos, kind of like double platforms.

My limited experience with still photos leads me to believe that it is of=
ten very difficult to see animals on the photos, particularly if there ar=
e any waves at all. You can usually detect something if you know there is=
 an animal in the photo (e.g. because it was detected by an observer at t=
he same time), but if you didn't know that, you would probably miss it.=20=

The photos should be useful for confirming group size and correcting dist=
ances, however.

You say that you have observers on each side who miss animals and who do =
not see animals that are not seen by the "good" observers. I guess we mig=
ht expect MRDS to estimate perfect detectability for the "good" observers=
 and poor detectability for the "bad" ones. Are the good observers always=
 on the same platform, or are they mixed? Are the platforms identical? If=
 so, you could put the good observers on a separate platform, despite the=
 actual seating position. If the observers are mixed, I guess you will en=
d up with g(0)<1 for both platforms. I am not sure which is the better wa=
y, I guess the overall combined g(0) will be the same.

Just some random thoughts, good luck.

Daniel Pike.

Reply 2:

September 27, 2011

You can use the photographic detections of animals to estimate the probab=
ility than a human observer detects an available animal in the overlap ar=
ea between human and camera search areas. To do this you do not need all =
photos or all photographed animals or all transect lines (unless transect=
 line was an explanatory variable for human detection probability, but I'=
m sure it is not). All you need is locations of a decent number of animal=
s detected photographically and whether or not these were detected by an =
observer. If you searched only photos in areas of high animal density and=
 used those as your trials in a Trial-observer MRDS configuration you'd g=
et an unbiased estimate of the human observers' detection functions - pro=
viding that there is nothing about the areas of high animal density that =
affects human observer detection probability. (If high density areas were=
 low Beaufort areas, for example, you'd be getting a positively biased es=
timate of observer detection probability overall.)

David

Reply 3:
October 1, 2011

Sounds like a good case for reviewing observer data while the survey is g=
oing on, to try to correct problems before it's too late!  Anyway, it's n=
ot a problem in theory to have different detection functions for differen=
t observers - you just need to estimate it.  But an alternative is to poo=
l the observations for the two observers on each side of the plane (so lo=
ng as duplicates are clear) so you're fitting a platform rather then obse=
rver specific model.

For the photo data, in theory there is no problem with focussing on trans=
ects where animals were seen to screen your photos.  Each narwhal you fin=
d on a photo represents a "trial" for the visual observers, and it doesn'=
t matter how you generate trials.  The assumption is that trial outcomes =
are independent in the double observer model, given the covariates.  Howe=
ver, in practice this is a bit dangerous because the double observer meth=
ods assume you get the detection function model right, and it might be th=
at something is affecting trackline detection probability in the low dens=
ity/low detectability transects that is not affecting it in the high dens=
ity/high detectability transects.  So, taking observations from just the =
high count transects seems dangerous.=20

 - len

Distance by default attempts to fit models with increasing number of adjust=
ments.  It often reaches a point where it is attempting to overfit the data=
, which is when you tend to see problems of this kind.  The solution is to =
use a simpler model, e.g. the one selected by AIC.  For small sample sizes,=
 this might often be the key function with no adjustment terms.

It means you're overfitting - see above.

If sample size is small (say up to 40 or 50 detections for a given species)=
, sampling fluctuations in the data can lead to poor models apparently fitt=
ing well.  You might want to consider using mcds with species included as a=
 factor-type covariate, allowing you to fit a single model to several (pref=
erably similar) species, while still allowing detectability to vary by spec=
ies.

With only 6 lines in your design, you don't have sufficient replication to =
extrapolate your results reliably to the wider region of interest - your in=
ference should really be restricted to just the 6 strips you surveyed.

We have used line transect survey methods to survey white-tailed deer in 3 =
study areas in South Florida.   Our density estimates have varied widely ov=
er the last 3 years and I am hoping to obtain some guidance on how to proce=
ed.

The survey areas are large (avg. 200 km2) and surveys are conducted using h=
elicopters.  The transects are placed in a parallel systematic grid at 1 km=
 intervals.   Distances are recorded in bins (0-25m, 25-50m, 50-100m, etc. =
up to 250+ meters).  In general, visibility is good, although there are por=
tions where the line is not visible due to thicker habitat.

Using one area as an example, the number of observations (clusters of deer)=
 have not changed much in the past years (143 to 179), however the abundanc=
e estimate has fluctuated from 810 deer in 2009 to 176 deer in 2011.  The r=
eason for this seems to be a change in the Effective Strip Width, which was=
 71 meters in 2009 and 300 meters (our cut off value) in 2011.   In 2009, t=
he histogram had a nice shoulder near the line, in 2010 there was some shou=
lder, and in 2011 the shape of the detection function was basically a strai=
ght line.  The pattern ; with very narrow ESW the first survey year and the=
 300 m ESW is seen in the other 2 areas also.  The overall number of observ=
ations has not changed much, basically just where the deer, in relation to =
the transect, are observed has changed.

Aerial surveys have been historically used in these areas due to large size=
 of the areas, low deer density, high visibility and inaccessibility by oth=
er means.   Aircraft used, observers, field methods (e.g. the way observers=
 search for deer, concentrating on the line) or visibility due to habitat h=
ave not changed in the past 3 years.

We don't want to give up on line transect survey methods, but at this point=
 it is difficult to use the data for management decisions.  We don't believ=
e that there has been a drastic change in the deer population in these area=
, in fact harvest numbers have increased in the last 3 years.  Could this d=
ue simply to sample size? It seems odd that by chance alone all 3 areas wou=
ld experience this shift in deer location (transects were created using GIS=
 and do not follow any landscape patterns).

Has anyone experienced something similar?  Any advice on how to proceed or =
anything we can change in our field methods or analyses to try to come up w=
ith a better estimate. We are considering mapping the sections of transects=
 where visibility is very low and eliminating those sections out of our sur=
vey, but I don't believe that would help us with our ESW issue.

Thank you,

mptions, and what may be going wrong.  So:

rded?  Has anything changed in those 3 years so that responsive movement is=
 causing greater bias in year 3 than in year 1?

3.  Have you had the same observers in all 3 years?  Have they searched in =
the same way each year (e.g. looking ahead of the helicopter, to detect ani=
mals before they move away from the helicopter vs. searching to the side, a=
nd only recording animals after responsive movement has started)?

vers have been recording animals beyond 300 m in 2011?  W=3D250m might be a=
 more reliable choice.

5.  Are animals culled by helicopter?  If so, is this a recent change?  (It=
 might result in animals responding by fleeing from the helicopter, and hen=
ce being recorded too far from the line after responsive movement has occur=
red, in 2011.)

If sample sizes are typically over 100 per year in each area, and you're se=
eing a consistent increase in ESW over the 3 years in each area, I agree th=
at this will not be due to sample size.  You need to understand what is cha=
nging to cause this ...

Steve

messages.subject: Re: model choice
messages.body_plain:
Quite right Matt.

Also, Brett, AIC is designed to account for the effect of additional parameters,
so all other things being equal, the lowest AIC model is the best choice.  As
Matt said, you need to check the model fit.  All of this is detailed in the
Introduction to Distance Sampling book - see particularly section 2.5 for advice
on how to proceed with analysis (this section is also in the Distance manual
(page on CDS Analysis Guidelines) and I think in the Thomas et al. (2010) paper
on Distance).

Note that it is not always advisable to choose the lowest AIC model, if you have
other reasons to think an alternative model produces more plausible estimates --
for an example of this that I'm familiar with, see the analysis for Pacific
white-sided dolphin in Williams and Thomas (2007).  Lastly, uncertainty about
detection function model selection can be incorporated into the analysis, via a
bootstrap (also in the Introduction to Distance sampling book somewhere; see
also the manual page on Model Averaging in CDS Analysis, and Williams and Thomas
(2009) for an example).

Cheers, - Len

messages.body_plain:
Malini:

You do have a difficult situation with aboreal mammals.  You might want=20
to have a look at some recent papers on surveys for this group of species=
:

  * Buckland, S.T., A.J. Plumptre, L. Thomas and E. Rexstad. 2010. Line
    transect sampling of primates: Can animal-to-observer distance
    methods work? International Journal of Primatology 31:485-499.
  * Buckland, S.T., A.J. Plumptre, L. Thomas and E. Rexstad. 2010.
    Design and analysis of line transect surveys for primates.
    International Journal of Primatology 31:833-847.

The topic of repeat visits to transects has been raised a few times on=20
this Distance list (for example 4 May 2009) where Tiago answers a=20
question like yours as:

"sightings you have in any given transect of length Lt, repeated k=20
times, and record the line length as being k*Lt. This tells Distance=20
that you have not been sampling k different transects, but the same=20
transect k times, and therefore Distance can calculate the appropriate=20
variances."  The 'pooling' term to which you refer means that you=20
include all sightings on a given regardless of visit as belonging to a=20
given transect (thereby pooling sightings over visits).

I would likely use study area as a 'stratum' in your Distance project.=20
In the sample (transect) layer of your project, you could include a=20
field (called 'visit') that would let you use the data filter in=20
Distance to explore your question of what happens as I reduce the number=20
of visits.  However you must remember to manually correct the length of=20
transect each time you filter out visits; because Distance needs to know=20
the total length of the transects walked to get encounter rate correct.

I realise you mention these are cut transects, but I cannot avoid=20
mention that 2, 3 or 4 transects per study area places you at a great=20
disadvantage for estimating variability in encounter rate between=20
transects.  You really need five times that many transects to get a good=20
understanding about how encounters vary between transects (and you need=20
this level of understanding to extrapolate from the parts of your study=20
area where you did survey to parts of the study area where you did not=20
survey).  I cannot imagine it is worth asking the question about how=20
estimates would be affected if you cut *fewer* transects.
